newsitem.title: CANADA: BANK OF MONTREAL REPORT SEES STRONG GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: BANK OF MONTREAL REPORT SEES STRONG GROWTH.

text.p: The Bank of Montreal on Wednesday said Canada will see strong economic growth in 1997 and 1998, boosted by employment growth and stronger consumer confidence.
Canada's third largest bank said it expects Canadian economic growth of 3.5 percent in 1997 and 3.7 percent in 1998. The forecasts were part of the bank's mid-year economic review.
The report notes that the Canadian economy now has a strong domestic impetus. Economic growth since the recession had been largely export driven.

"We're expecting at least 700,000 jobs to be created this year and next, reducing the unemployment rate to an average of 8.7 percent in 1998," Tim O'Neill, Bank of Montreal chief economist said in a statement.

The bank forecast that the Canadian dollar will appreciate through the rest of 1997 and 1998, though it will remain undervalued and continue to be supportive of Canadian exporters. The bank also expects short-term Canadian interest rates to rise, but said low interest rates in general will continue providing stimulus for the economy.
Canadian governments at both the federal and provincial level are expected to provide modest tax relief and selective spending increases, the bank said.

On the provincial front, Alberta is expected to lead economic growth in Canada in the next two years, with a robust energy sector helping the oil-rich province grow 4.3 percent in 1997 and 4.5 percent in 1998.

In Ontario, Canada's most populous province, the economy is expected to grow by 3.9 percent his year and 4.0 percent in 1998. The French-speaking province of Quebec is seen growing by 2.8 percent in 1997 and 3.2 percent in 1998.
British Columbia is expected to grow by 2.6 percent his year and 3.5 percent in 1998.
The remaining Canadian provinces except for Prince Edward Island are expected to post economic growth both this year and next.
